excerpt_original: In Monomyths, Chidy Wayne turns to distorted figures, layered surfaces, and recurring archetypes to explore identity and inheritance.

blocks.text: Southern Guild, a South African gallery, just opened its New York outpost in April. Right now, they have two exhibitions up: sculptural wool works on canvas by Moroccan artist Amine El Gotaibi in the front gallery, and paintings by Spanish-Guinean artist Chidy Wayne in the back. Both are excellent. Wayne’s paintings revolve around a recurring male figure, which the press release identifies as inspired by both the artist’s father and his own likeness. Together, these paternal and autobiographical presences become fractured iterations of masculine archetypes, continually being dismantled and reassembled.

The works on view belong to Wayne’s Pugnatores series, whose title derives from the Latin word pugna , meaning “fight.” The figures reflect the artist’s struggle to reconcile questions of identity and purpose.
